Lastre Research · Strategy document

Proof before value: rare earths, Brazil, and the provenance layer

Asymmetric information, verification at zero marginal cost, the country case of Brazilian rare earths, and the construction of a multi-channel rail of proof and settlement for real-world assets.

Lastre Research · August 2026 · São Paulo — Zug
Internal · restricted circulation · data verified as of 08/08/2026 · the model in Part II §9 is parametric and illustrative
Abstract

Markets for physical assets operate under structural information asymmetry: the seller knows the asset's origin; the buyer does not. When verification is expensive, the provenance premium cannot hold and the market converges to the low-quality equilibrium described by Akerlof. This article formalizes Lastre as a technology for lowering the cost of verification and raising the cost of fraud — the two frontiers that define the separating equilibrium — implemented as a multi-channel rail of proof and settlement: a physical reading sealed offline by deterministic hash, anchored on a public chain, with a permanent binary verdict as the precondition of any issuance.

We show (i) why the deterministic verdict dominates oracles and API attestations in the incentive structure; (ii) that the seal transports truth but does not originate it, which localizes residual risk at the physical boundary and determines the anchoring policy; (iii) a taxonomy of sixteen backable asset classes ordered by measurability of origin and regulatory pressure, with five dated regulatory milestones between December 2026 and 2028 that create an obligated buyer; (iv) the country case of Brazilian rare earths — the refining bottleneck, the arithmetic of verticalization, and the 20%-to-48% realization premium that only exists with proven origin — as the rail's first channel; (v) a parametric revenue model — take-rate on backed GMV, verification quotas and subscriptions — with the relevant elasticities; and (vi) the strategic sequence feed → rail → standard, with the LBMA/aXedras and Tracr/GIA precedents as evidence that the full arrangement is viable.

Internal strategy document · Lastre Research · August 2026. Market data verified against primary sources as of the 08/08/2026 cutoff; qualitative assessments and the parametric model are our own derivation and are marked as such. Not an investment offering; Lastre confers proof, not ownership.

Part I
The country thesis

Rare earths and Brazil's future — full text: the map of power, China, the real Brazil, the six locks, the Western bloc, the audit of the bets, the platform company, the economics of the thesis, the roadmap and the tracking panel.

—Opening

Executive summary

What changed, what fell apart, and what needs to replace it.

What was confirmed

The bottleneck thesis is right and has become sharper. China does not dominate because it has ore: it holds 69% of mining, but 91% of separation, 94% of sintered magnets and about 99% of heavy rare earth separation. Outside China, existing and announced capacity will cover in 2035 only half of mining demand, a quarter of refining demand and less than a fifth of magnet demand. The magnet gap is four times larger than the mine gap — and Brazil keeps aiming at the mine.

What fell apart

Version 1's Bet 2 — clean energy as a competitive advantage in refining — does not survive the data. Rare earth separation is intensive in reagent and capital, not in electricity: in a full life-cycle assessment of an NdFeB magnet, electricity consumption in sintering and processing has an impact described as negligible, and rare earth metals account for about 90% of the footprint. Energy is on the order of 1% to 3% of the operating cost of a separation plant. And the hardest proof is revealed preference: two projects with Brazilian ore chose to refine outside Brazil — Serra Verde in France, Aclara in Louisiana — and Aclara literally uses the clean grid of Goiás as a marketing argument while installing the value-added step in a US state run on gas and nuclear.

What replaces it

The asset Brazil has not priced is not the clean electron. It is three other things, and all three are actionable within a political time frame: (1) heavy rare earths from ionic clay with easy desorption — the only segment where China is nearly irreplaceable and where Brazil has first-rate geology; (2) the Uberaba phosphogypsum, an already concentrated environmental liability that can become nearly 2,000 t/yr of NdPr oxide without opening a new mine; (3) buyer power, not seller power — the ability to condition access to the asset, which is exactly what the Brazilian state failed to exercise three times in a row.

The conclusion that reorganizes everything

Brazilian verticalization does not pay for itself. On the section 12 modeling estimate, a complete national module turns a cash profit from a magnet realized at US$ 81/kg, remunerates concessional capital at US$ 107/kg and market capital at US$ 126/kg. The reference used is US$ 85/kg. The distance between unviable and viable is a realization premium of 20% to 48% on the magnet — within the 25% to 67% range that the market outside China already practices on separated oxides.

In other words: the decisive instrument Brazil lacks is not money — BNDES and FINEP have already pre-selected R$ 45.8 billion. It is price floor and long-term offtake. That is exactly what the United States gave MP Materials, what Japan gave Lynas, and what Australia is building. And it is exactly what Serra Verde handed to a US government SPV for fifteen years, with no Brazilian legal framework in place to review the transaction.

CHAPTER 02Diagnosis

The map of power

Power is not distributed along the chain. It is stacked in three links.

The reserves table is the wrong metric and the most cited one. What decides is where the chain chokes. Below, the Chinese share link by link — the same chain, four very different concentrations.

Against that backdrop, Brazil's position is less a paradox than a sequence of choices. The country holds between 15% and 25% of world reserves depending on the accounting criterion, half a percent of production, and none of the separation capacity.

The two-price market

The most important consequence of the Chinese controls is not scarcity — it is the price bifurcation, and it is structural. The IEA records that in Europe gallium and heavy rare earths cost about five times the Chinese domestic price. S&P Global calculates that Chinese refined compounds come out five to six times cheaper than those produced in the West. The pattern is asymmetric. Measured in March 2026, the FOB premium over the Chinese domestic price was 63% in neodymium oxide, 67% in dysprosium and 47% in terbium; other, more conservative series put the premium on lights at 10% to 25%. In heavies, depending on the market and the window, it runs from 2 to 12 times. For dysprosium and terbium, in fact, the sentence that describes the market is not about price — it is availability trumps price. It is rationing, not price formation. Throughout this document I use the conservative range of 25% to 67% as a benchmark for the premium charged outside China.

Where the value is

If there is a single chart that should guide Brazilian policy, it is this one. Not the reserves chart.

And the gap the West still has to fill is precisely at the end of the chain, not at the beginning:

In short
  • China holds 69% of mining but 91% of separation and 94% of magnets. The mine is the replicable link; the rest is not.
  • Brazil holds between 15% and 25% of world reserves, 0.51% of production and no separation plant at all.
  • The 2035 global gap is in the magnet (82% uncovered), not in the mine (50%).
CHAPTER 03The adversary

China

The control architecture, the November calendar, and the five cracks.

Between December 2023 and August 2026, Beijing assembled the most sophisticated instrument of economic coercion since the oil embargo — and then partially suspended it. Understanding what is in force today matters more than the entire chronology.

What holds as of August 8, 2026

The announcement numbers below come from secondary legal analyses (Taylor Wessing, Clark Hill, Han Kun, Morgan Lewis, Greenberg Traurig) and from Global Trade Alert compilations, not from direct translation of MOFCOM. The measures are well documented; the numbering is the weakest link. estimate

  • Announcement 18/2025 — case-by-case licensing for seven medium and heavy elements (samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium) and everything containing them, including magnets. Permanent, never suspended.
  • Technology ban of Dec/2023 — export of extraction, separation and metal and alloy production technology is prohibited; the magnet manufacturing one, restricted. This is the most durable item in the arsenal: it does not expire, it was not part of any truce, and it is the one that hurts most over the long run.
  • Announcement 1/2026 — blocking of dual-use items to Japan whenever they expand Japanese military capacity, triggered by Prime Minister Takaichi's statement on Taiwan. The first time Beijing has explicitly linked mineral control to a foreign policy position on Taiwan.
  • Entity lists — 10 US companies on 22/06/2026, including MP Materials and USA Rare Earth; 20 Japanese ones on 29/06; 14 European ones on 24/07; drone-related items destined for the US on 05/08/2026.

What is suspended — and the date that organizes the next six months

The harshest announcements of October 2025 — among them the 0.1% rule, which would require a Chinese license for any product made outside China containing 0.1% by value of Chinese rare earth, and the technical documentation control — are suspended until November 10, 2026. The ban on gallium, germanium and antimony to the US, until 27 November.

Free access to most markets, reduction to the US, restriction to Japan — three simultaneous regimes.

Where China bleeds

  1. Myanmar, and it is the crack that no amount of capital closes. Northern Kachin State accounts for somewhere between half and 70% of global heavy rare earths supply outside China's domestic quota — 370 mining sites and roughly 2,700 leaching ponds. In October 2024 the Kachin Independence Army took Pangwa and Chipwi; Chinese imports of Burmese ore fell 89% in February 2025, and the KIO began charging an export fee of ~US$ 4,800 per tonne. Burmese production fell from 27,000 t (2024) to 22,000 t (2025). China deliberately pushed dirty extraction beyond its own borders — and the price was turning geological risk into geopolitical risk.
  2. The lever consumes itself. Every squeeze accelerates the building of the alternative. The evidence is direct: after the Department of Defense injection, MP Materials raised US$ 1 billion with J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs. Chinese coercion created the private market that did not exist before.
  3. The environmental liability has become a growth ceiling. The Weikuang tailings dam, in Baotou, holds about 10 km² of lead, cadmium and radioactive thorium, built in the 1950s with no impermeable liner. The MIIT estimated the environmental damage at ¥ 38 billion as far back as 2011. Mining quota growth slowed from +21.4% (2023) to +5.9% (2024). China cannot expand aggressively at home.
  4. The 0.1% rule is practically unauditable. Once outside China, rare earths become indistinguishable after being processed or alloyed. Verifying 0.1% by value in a magnet embedded in a motor embedded in a car is, in practice, unworkable — the regime depends on border control and licensing discretion, not on real traceability.
  5. It needs to sell. China exports about 58 thousand tonnes of magnets a year. A total restriction would destroy revenue, jobs and — more importantly — the default supplier position that sustains the entry barrier.
Where China is not vulnerable — to calibrate the optimism

Heavies separation: ~99%. Lynas produced the first commercial dysprosium oxide outside China only in May 2025. Separation and magnet technology has been under an export ban since December 2023, with no relief and no deadline. And a structural deficit estimated at ~44 thousand tonnes/year of NdPr remains, which only China supplies.

4.2 Actual refining capacity: zero industrial

Everything that exists in Brazil in separation, metallization and magnets fits in a short table, and nothing in it is industrial.

  • CIT SENAI ITR, Lagoa Santa (MG) — NdFeB magnet laboratory-factory, the first in the Southern Hemisphere, with a pilot plant inaugurated in December 2025. Maximum nominal capacity of 100 t/yr, admittedly unlikely to be reached because the focus is research. Estimated mastery of 60% to 70% of the technology cycle.
  • March 1, 2026 — the milestone: Meteoric delivered 20 kg of rare earth carbonate to CIT SENAI — every 600 kg of clay yields about 2 kg of carbonate. It was the first time a magnet was produced in Brazil with domestic ore. Until then the laboratory used imported Chinese material.
  • CETEM (RJ) — separation of Pr and Nd by solvent extraction, with a patent granted in 2022. Critical limitation: it works with synthetic solutions, not with real mineral concentrate.
  • IPT (SP) — electrochemical reduction pilot reactor of ~1 kg/h. UFSC — 42 MGOe magnets in the laboratory, against 55 MGOe for the commercial standard.
  • MagBras — program launched in July 2025, R$ 73 million, 38 entities, target of consolidating the chain by 2030.

4.3 The State's three omissions

The sale of Serra Verde was not a regulatory accident. It was the third consecutive moment in which the federal Executive could have acted and chose not to.

  1. 2010 — the concession with nothing in return. The license was granted with no local processing requirement whatsoever. Serra Verde, in fact, already was 100% foreign capital before the deal with the Americans — Denham Capital, Vision Blue and Energy & Minerals Group. Much of the "selling off sovereignty" narrative ignores this.
  2. August 2025 — the DFC loan. The US agency approved US$ 465 million for Serra Verde without any statement from Itamaraty at the time.
  3. April 2026 — the sale. The ANM authorized the transfer of control with no public national interest review. CADE did not open a case on its own initiative — it only opened the proceeding on 11/05/2026, after a complaint filed by a congressman. The MME and Itamaraty made no formal statement. The reaction came from the Legislature and the STF (an ADPF filed by Rede Sustentabilidade), not from the Executive. And the government of Goiás, which later criticized the deal, had signed a cooperation memorandum with the US in March 2026 and created a critical minerals authority by state law.

In interviews with the Brazilian press in April 2026, Serra Verde's CEO acknowledged that the American buyer does not guarantee supply to the Brazilian market and that all initial production is committed under a fifteen-year contract.

Paraphrase of statements to the press, April 2026 — not a verbatim quote

4.4 The two bottlenecks nobody discusses

The nuclear monopoly

The Constitution and Law 4.118/1962 give the Union a monopoly over nuclear ores. Monazite is a phosphate of cerium, lanthanum, neodymium and thorium. Legally, therefore, a rare earths project in monazite is a nuclear mineral project, regardless of whether the intent is a magnet rather than a reactor. The empirical proof that the lock was real: in April 2026 ADL Mineração made Brazil's first private monazite shipment in decades, bound for Canada. Law 14.514/2022 opened a contractual valve via INB, but pending regulation — it turned a ban into administrative discretion, which for investment decision purposes can be worse, because it is neither auditable nor time-bound. And even unlocked, the material leaves raw: what is missing is the separation plant, not the license.

The counterargument any liberalization proposal has to anticipate is Kvanefjeld: Greenland passed a zero-tolerance uranium law in 2021, killed the project, and the company sought US$ 7.5 billion in arbitration — and lost, with the tribunal declaring it had no jurisdiction. Thorium regulatory risk is structurally uninsurable.

The map that does not exist

Probably the most underestimated bottleneck on the entire agenda, and the cheapest to fix. The Geological Survey of Brazil needs R$ 80 million per year in airborne geophysical surveys. It received R$ 8 million in the new 2026 PAC — 10% of what is needed. In 2025 it was R$ 17 million, cut to ~R$ 11 million after budget cuts. At the current pace, according to the SGB's own director, Brazil would take "more than a hundred years" to properly map its reserves. And he is explicit about the nature of the problem: is not a technical limitation, it is budget. The improvised workaround has been state co-financing — Tocantins closed 20,300 km² for R$ 10.4 million, with priority access to the data.

The disproportion that sums up Brazilian public policy

R$ 45.8 billion pre-selected by BNDES and FINEP for strategic mineral transformation. R$ 8 million to find out where the minerals are.

4.5 Public policy arrived after the capital

The chronology matters more than the content. The BNDES/FINEP call received R$ 85.2 bn in proposals and pre-selected 56 projects, R$ 45.8 bn — of which 10 in rare earths — before the National Rare Earths Strategy exists (MME/CEBRI/BID study published on 19/06/2026, still not turned into a decree) and before the National Critical Minerals Policy is law. Observatório da Mineração notes that the business plans are confidential and that environmental and social compliance was pushed to the second phase — money can be released before the check.

What PL 2780 delivers concretely, if and when it passes: the CIMCE, a council attached to the Presidency (under which the sale of Serra Verde would have required approval); the FGAM, a guarantee fund with up to R$ 2 bn in federal capitalization; R$ 5 bn in tax credits of up to 20% of capex in processing, over the 2030–2034 period; incentivized debentures; and contributions of 0.2% of revenue to the FGAM and 0.3% to R&D. What it does not bring: an obligation of domestic value addition, a foreign investment screening mechanism on the Canadian or Australian model, free, prior and informed consultation under ILO Convention 169 — the text speaks of "continuous and transparent dialogue", which is not the same thing — and nothing about CFEM for rare earths.

In short
  • Serra Verde was sold for US$ 2.8 bn with a 15-year offtake and no refining commitment in Brazil.
  • The state could have acted three times — concession, DFC loan, sale — and acted in none of them.
  • Two invisible locks: the nuclear monopoly over monazite and a mapping budget at 10% of what is needed.
CHAPTER 05What blocks it

The six locks

What Brazil lacks is not ore, energy or money. It is people, rules and deadlines.

This section did not exist in version 1 and is the one whose shape changed most with the research. The intuition — "what is missing is the as" — is right. What the data adds is the hierarchy: the locks do not carry the same weight, and the first of them explains almost all the others.

  1. Technological mastery of separation — the master lock, and it is measurable. Out of a universe of 281 solvent extraction patents of rare earths filed between 2010 and 2019, China has 89, the United States 78, Japan 47 — and Brazil has two. One from CNEN, in 2014; the other from CETEM, in 2016. Both public, neither industrialized. In the broad rare earth universe, there are 48,112 patents worldwide, of which China holds 62% and Brazil 56. Half of Brazilian filings are for individual.

    CGEE names the bottleneck without euphemism in its July 2026 study: "absence of operational mastery of solvent extraction circuits" combined with a "lack of analytical and radiological infrastructure." And ComCiência's diagnosis is even more direct: in Brazil, rare earths separation is done only by academic institutions.
  2. Training pipeline — the country trains 902 people per year for the entire mineral processing chain. 2023 graduates, per the Higher Education Census: Chemical Engineering 4.328, Materials Engineering 580, Mining Engineering 322. And the engineering total as a whole fell 25.8% in five years — from 128,871 in 2018 to 95,607 in 2023.

    On the other side: China has at least 11 institutions with a specific undergraduate program in rare earths, more than 500 students a year in those programs and more than 40 specialized laboratories. The United States, which has no dedicated undergraduate program and graduated barely 200 mining and metallurgical engineers in 2023, responded in August 7, 2026 with US$ 180 million in mining education alone — US$ 100 mn from the DOE through the PROSPECT program and more than US$ 80 mn from the Department of War, with a stated target of double the number of graduates in two years.

    The Brazilian response, on the same scale: R$ 73 million at MagBras — which is an industrial demonstrator, not a training program — and R$ 10.2 million over five years at INCT MATERIA. And there is no public statistic on how many masters and doctorates Brazil awards per year in hydrometallurgy or solvent extraction. The last census of rare earths research groups dates from 2013.
  3. The State's regulatory capacity — the ANM operates with 61% staffing shortfall. These are 743 active staff for 1,930 authorized positions, and about 25% of those who remain are on leave. The result, per the Tribunal de Contas da União itself: 68 thousand pending applications, 800 mines idle for about 14 years awaiting review, 17 mining companies inspected in 2022 out of more than 39 thousand cases, and potential CFEM losses of up to R$ 12.4 billion. The TCU describes the situation as "extreme precariousness".

    This is not an administrative detail: it is the reason the state has not been able — and will not be able — to impose conditionality on transactions like Serra Verde's. A state without people imposes no safeguard.
  4. Permitting predictability — improved on paper, and there is still no list. The Special Environmental License did not come by Law 15.190/2025 — it was vetoed there and recreated by MP 1.308/2025, converted into Law 15.300/2025, in force since 23/12/2025. It consolidates the three phases into one and sets a maximum deadline of 12 months. The body that decides the classification is the Câmara de Atividades e Empreendimentos Estratégicos (Decree 12.673/2025), coordinated by the Casa Civil, with eleven ministries — and the decree sets no deadline for it to rule. As of August 2026 there is no published list of qualified projects, although the MME has drafted a resolution to bring critical minerals in.

    And the backdrop: there is no official statistic of average mining permitting time in Brazil. The figure in circulation is a market estimate — 3 to 4 years, against 18 to 24 months in competing jurisdictions. Brazil does not even appear in the S&P Global sample on discovery-to-production time, whose global average is 15.7 years and has risen to about 30 years because of permitting delays.
  5. Infrastructure and logistics costs — 15.5% of GDP, and worsening. Brazilian logistics costs rose from 10.4% of GDP in 2014 to 15.5% in 2025 — more than five percentage points in eleven years, with the inventory component going from 3% to 5%. The country moves about 25% more freight with practically the same physical base.

    And there is one figure nobody has calculated: there is no public study that quantifies energy demand in MW and water demand in m³/s for a rare earths separation hub in Brazil, nor an availability report for Goiás or southern Minas. For a thesis that leans on energy, that is a hole. The international benchmark is harsh: separation consumes 9 to 13 times the energy of extraction, and the monazite route uses about 11,170 kg of water per kg of rare earth.

    There is no integrated federal hub. What exists is subnational: Goiás published a decree on 08/06/2026 creating AMIC/GO, special zones, a state fund and — the most interesting instrument in the country today — a Progressive Verticalization Plan which conditions incentives on refining targets in the state, capping at 50% the activities carried out elsewhere. It is the safeguard missing from PL 2780, written by a state government.
  6. Patient capital — it exists, and demand is nine times greater. The BNDES critical minerals line comes at 6.5% a year on the investment portion, with a final cost of 8% to 11% depending on risk, a term of up to 20 years and a grace period of up to 4 — a ceiling of R$ 500 million per economic group. Brasil Soberano 3, of 22/07/2026, brought R$ 18.5 billion and a critical minerals processing credit line at 3% a year, the smallest in the program. And BNDESPar came in as a shareholder: the FIP Ore Régia, with Vale, targets up to R$ 1 billion in junior explorers.

    The problem is not the absence of an instrument. It is proportion: the mineral transformation call received 124 business plans, US$ 16 billion of stated intent, and pre-selected R$ 45.8 billion against a budget initially forecast at R$ 5 billion. Nine to one. Meanwhile, the Selic at 14% makes any project that only generates cash in 2029–2031 almost ineligible for domestic private capital — which is exactly why all the real money that has entered the Brazilian sector is foreign.
The safeguard PL 2780 does not see

No rare earths separation plant operates without a radiological license: monazite and much of the clay carry thorium and uranium, and the residue is permanent. The PL 2780 does not mention CNEN nor does it set a standard for residual thorium and uranium. Malaysia has just shown what that costs: in renewing Lynas's license for ten years in March 2026, it required the company to cease radioactive waste production within five years, neutralize everything below 1 Bq/g and build no new permanent disposal facilities.

It is the political ceiling of any refinery — and in Brazil it is not even written down.

In short
  • The master lock is technical: two Brazilian solvent-extraction patents against 89 Chinese ones.
  • Brazil graduates 902 people a year in Materials and Mining; China has 11 universities dedicated to rare earths.
  • ANM runs with a 61% staffing shortfall and 68,000 pending cases — a state without people cannot impose a lock.
CHAPTER 06The board

The Western bloc

US$ 110 per kilo has become the West's Schelling point. And there is an empty seat.

The most important fact about the Western response is not the volume of money — it is the spontaneous convergence to a price. Three independent agreements, with no formal treaty, settled on the same number.

The money, to give a sense of scale

More than US$ 7.3 billion committed by five US agencies; € 64 billion announced across 195 critical minerals supply chain projects since the start of 2026, according to the G7; US$ 12.7 billion in Project Vault, the US strategic reserve run as a public-private partnership with Hartree, Traxys and Mercuria as buying agents and Boeing, GE Vernova and Western Digital among the participating OEMs. In Europe, the Caremag in Lacq — € 216 million, part of it coming from Japan — will produce 600 t/yr of Dy + Tb, against the 140 t/yr Energy Fuels is targeting in Utah. In heavies, Europe is further ahead than the US. estimate — the company presents the 600 t/a as "~15% of world production", which does not square with estimated global Dy+Tb supply (500 to 900 t/yr); the counting bases diverge and I could not reconcile them.

The empty seat

Brazil is not a member of the G7 Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance — the only forum that formally discusses quotas, price floors, joint offtake and coordinated stockpiling. Brazil took part in the Critical Minerals Ministerial of 04/02/2026 and is cited as a partner of the former MSP, but it is outside the core. Meanwhile, its assets got in: US$ 565 mn from the DFC in Serra Verde, a US$ 250 mn EXIM LOI to Meteoric, a JOGMEC MOU with the state of Goiás in March 2026, Solvay's LOI with Viridis in June.

The pattern is unambiguous: Brazil is supplying the asset without being at the table where the asset's price is set.

And there is one figure that repositions the entire negotiation: the United States raised the tariff on Brazil to 37.5% cumulative in July 2026, in two separate actions — 25% published on 20/07 and another 12.5% on 28/07 — and the USTR proposal that underpinned the first explicitly excluded critical minerals: iron ore, graphite, niobium, rare earths, copper, nickel, and processed forms as well, among them ferroniobium, rare earth metals and lithium compounds. estimate — the final annexes were published as an image in the Federal Register and the definitive list could not be checked item by item. The logic, however, is clear: the tariff is a pincer, not a wall. You tax what you can substitute and exempt what you need. At the same time, a Brazilian diplomat summed up Lula's May 2026 visit to Washington by saying that "there is nothing ready to be signed" — Brazil demands processing on national territory before export and refuses exclusivity; the US demands guarantees against Chinese manipulation. There is no bilateral critical minerals agreement between Brazil and the USA.

CHAPTER 07Audit

Audit of the five bets

Two are confirmed, one fails, one partially fails and one changes in nature.

Bet 1 — Do not sell ore, sell the magnet · confirmed and reinforced

It remains the right bet, and now there are numbers behind it: a ×4.4 multiplier from concentrate to magnet, an 82% gap in magnet capacity outside China in 2035, and 85% of the chain disappearing between the mine and the magnet. What version 1 did not say is how much this costs and under what condition it closes — is in section 12, and the answer is uncomfortable.

Bet 2 — Clean energy as a competitive advantage · failed as formulated

This is the most important correction in the document. The thesis does not survive four independent facts.

  1. Separation is not electricity-intensive. It is intensive in acid, base, organic solvent and capital — cascades of hundreds to thousands of mixer-settler stages, and about 10 t of HCl per tonne of REO. In a life cycle analysis of an NdFeB magnet, "sintering, magnetization and electricity consumption had negligible impacts"; rare earth metals account for about 90% of emissions. Energy is on the order of 1% to 3% of OPEX of separation.
  2. The footprint difference comes from the mineralogical route, not from the wall socket. Neodymium oxide: southern China 52, Bayan Obo 31, Mountain Pass 34, Mount Weld 14 kg of CO₂ per kg. The best performance is from an Australian plant powered by natural gas.
  3. There is no green premium for rare earths. No index, no priced certification, and no carbon regulatory obligation for magnets. CBAM entered its definitive regime on 01/01/2026 and covers six sectors — cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. Does not cover magnets or rare earths, nor in the expansion proposed for 2028. A Brazilian magnet made with 100% renewable energy receives no CBAM benefit. And where the green premium does exist, it is minuscule: low-carbon aluminum, US$ 0–25 per tonne on ~US$ 2,945 — up to 0.85%; nickel, 488 tonnes traded in two years; copper, zero. Only steel has a material premium, and only in Europe, in premium automotive, in less than 0.25% of world production.
  4. Revealed preference. Aclara literally uses the phrase "low carbon footprint driven by the 100% renewable grid of Goiás" — and installed separation in Lake Charles, Louisiana, whose grid is gas and nuclear. Serra Verde sends its concentrate to France. Two projects with Brazilian ore, zero refining in Brazil.

And the argument that Brazilian energy is cheap for industrial users does not hold as stated. It is cheap in the molecule and expensive on the bill: R$ 233/MWh in the long-term free market (≈ US$ 43/MWh) against R$ 785/MWh in the average captive industrial tariff (≈ US$ 145/MWh). Forty-four and a half percent of the industrial bill is neither energy nor wires — it is charges and taxes. The CDE grew from R$ 14.1 bn (2013) to R$ 49.2 bn (2025).

What remains true in Bet 2, and it is not little: Brazil's power mix é genuinely clean — 87.2% of capacity and 89% of generation — and that is a attribute of social license and of future compliance, not a price premium. It serves to pass IRMA and battery passport due diligence, to avoid being blocked, to avoid losing a European customer. It is a condition of entry, not a competitive advantage. Selling it as an advantage is the mistake; abandoning it would be one too.

Corollary: complementarity with AI data centers does not exist

A rare earths separation plant requires something like 5 MW; MP Materials' entire integrated complex at Mountain Pass, 26 MW. A hyperscale AI campus runs from 100 to 750 MW. The ratio runs from 1-to-20 to 1-to-150, and the 7,040 MW of data centers already approved by the ONS are equivalent to 1,408 separation plants. Worse: the two profiles are baseload, so there is no load-factor gain — there is competition for the same scarcity, which is grid connection capacity. In Ceará this is already literal: the ONS turned down R$ 115 billion in projects because of corridor saturation. And in a fight for connection the data center always wins, because the value per MW of AI compute is orders of magnitude higher than that of rare earth oxide.

Add the geographic mismatch: 78.5% of the curtailment is in the Northeast; 56% of approved data center MW are in São Paulo. And the locational driver of the AI data center is speed-to-power, not price-of-power — energy is ~10% to 12% of the annualized cost of a rack that depreciates in four years. Brazil offers the second-order variable and fails on the first-order one.

Bet 3 — Decentralized and inverted technology · partially failed

Three components, three different verdicts.

  • Modular refining — it exists, but it has scale floor. On the comparables, the smallest defensible size for full chemical separation in a market economy is 1,000 to 2,000 t/yr: Aclara Dynamo (~1,300 t/a, US$ 277 mn) and Rainbow Phalaborwa (~2,070 t/a, US$ 326 mn). Below that it only exists with a military offtake or a subsidy — Phoenix Tailings produces 200 kg/ano today, targets 120 t by 2027–28 and has a US$ 500 mn loan from the Department of War. And "modular" in this sector almost always means "building the same module several times", not "a small plant at the mine mouth". Solvay, which has the mature plant, says in plain terms that the problem is not capacity — it is having a customer committed to buying locally.
  • Bioleaching — is not a path for primary ore. Yields of 20% to 50% in a bench-scale bioreactor, glucose accounting for 44% of OPEX, experiments with 500 mg samples. The niche is tailings, spent catalyst and phosphogypsum. First industrial pilot no earlier than 2029–2031; material contribution to global supply, after 2035 if it happens.
  • Urban mining — here version 1 was right and underestimated the reason. Rare earth recycling today is less than 1%, and physics locks it: there is a ~12-year lag between making the magnet and it becoming scrap. Even in the aggressive scenario, recycling covers ~8% of demand in 2030, and the European 25% target falls 17 points short. The real gains come from factory scrap, not of installed stock — conflating the two is the central error of the urban mining argument. But tailings are another story, and it is the best Brazilian news in the document. See section 8.

Bet 4 — Foreign investment with a safeguard · confirmed and now urgent

Version 1 said that PL 2780 "tries to create" the safeguard. It does not. Value addition enters through a tax incentive, not through an obligation; there is no ban on exporting concentrate, no requirement of local processing as a condition of the license, and no foreign investment screening mechanism equivalent to Australia's FIRB or the Canadian regime — a gap flagged by the Senate's own Legislative Bulletin, which cites both as comparisons. Serra Verde is the proof of concept of that absence: asset sold, a 15-year offtake, price floors for the buyer, and no industrial quid pro quo in the country of origin.

The Australian precedent shows the safeguard is enforceable: the Treasurer issued forced divestment orders covering ~17.6% of Northern Minerals' equity held by shareholders linked to China, on national security grounds. This is not about scaring capital away — it is about pricing access.

Bet 5 — Becoming the axis of the non-Chinese bloc · correct, but the club has already formed

Version 1 proposed creating a "rare earths OPEC". It already exists in three overlapping layers — the G7 Alliance (production and floors), FORGE (geopolitical partnerships, successor to the MSP, launched on 04/02/2026 under the South Korean presidency, which passed to the United States in July 2026) and Project Vault (stockpile and buyers' club). Brazil is outside the first, peripheral in the second, absent from the third. The bet changes in nature: it is no longer establish the bloc, is negotiate entry with whatever bargaining power is still left — and what there is is heavies geology and the fact that the bloc needs non-Chinese volume before 2030.

CHAPTER 08What was missing

The three bets that were missing

Where Brazil has a real advantage, and not just a narrative one.

  1. Heavies — the only segment where China is close to irreplaceable. Dysprosium and terbium together account for something around 0.15% of world rare earth volume and concentrate bargaining power disproportionately: China holds ~99% of heavy separation, the price outside China runs to several times the Chinese domestic price, and global terbium supply is somewhere between 100 and 400 t/yr, with a projected deficit of 400 to 700 t/yr in 2035. Current supply comes from ionic clays in southern China and northern Myanmar under militia control. Brazil has ionic clay with elevated Tb and Dy — the USGS's own heavies chapter singles out Serra Verde for this. The entire strategy should be recalibrated around heavies, not NdPr.

    The counterargument, and it is a serious one: it is also in heavies that the demand destruction risk is greatest. Proterial launched in July 2025 a sintered neodymium magnet without heavy rare earths — it eliminates Dy and Tb while keeping Nd and Pr. This is not "rare-earth-free": it is surgical de-risking of the real bottleneck. Grain boundary diffusion goes in the same direction. Long theses on Dy/Tb with a ten-year horizon are the most exposed in the sector.
  2. Uberaba phosphogypsum — the most concrete Brazilian asset, and almost no one is looking at it. Mosaic and Rainbow Rare Earths published an Economic Assessment in March 2026 to process 2.7 Mt/yr of phosphogypsum in Uberaba, producing 1,971 t/yr of NdPr oxide and 659 t/yr of SEG+ product — which includes 60 t of dysprosium, 14 t of terbium and 188 t of yttrium. CAPEX of US$ 279 mn, post-tax NPV of US$ 916 mn, payback of 1.7 years. PFS and DFS in 2026, construction in 2027, first production in 2030.

    Why this is different from everything else on the list: mine CAPEX is approximately zero — the fertilizer infrastructure already exists, the material is already ground and concentrated, and it is a environmental liability, not a resource to be opened. The direct comparable is Phalaborwa, in South Africa, where ANSTO confirmed that it takes only two small solvent extraction circuits, ~75 mixer-settlers, because phosphogypsum arrives already enriched and without problematic thorium — against the hundreds to thousands of stages of a conventional cascade. Phalaborwa projects OPEX of US$ 40.83/kg of separated magnetic oxide, NPV of US$ 611 mn and payback of 2.0 years. It is the shortest route Brazil has to a separation plant on domestic soil, and it does not depend on opening any new mine.
  3. Buyer power, not seller power. Version 1's mental frame was that of an exporter looking for a market. The 2026 evidence suggests the opposite: the world needs the Brazilian asset before of 2030 and has no near alternative. The US exempted rare earths from the 37.5% tariff. Japan signed an MOU with the state of Goiás. Solvay signed an LOI with Viridis. EXIM issued a US$ 250 mn LOI to Meteoric. The DFC put US$ 565 mn into Serra Verde. Five jurisdictions came to take, and none was required to leave anything in return.

    That is buyer power left unused. The matching instrument is neither a tariff nor a state-owned company — it is access conditionality: approval of a change-of-control transaction tied to a commitment to separate on national territory, with a deadline and a penalty; mandatory participation in an R&D consortium; a reserved share of production for the domestic chain. It is what Canada and Australia do through national security screening, and what PL 2780, in its current text, does not do.
CHAPTER 09The idea

The platform company

The right idea, tested against what the sector actually does. Two of the three do not survive in the form proposed.

The logic is sound and worth stating without the jargon: do not own the commodity, own the point everyone has to pass through. Applied to rare earths, that means building the bottleneck the West will have to cross to escape China. The question is whether any of the three proposed formats survives contact with the evidence.

Idea 1 — The refinery as a platform does not survive in pure form

The proposal: a plant that takes concentrate from any mine in the non-Chinese bloc, returns separated oxide or magnets and charges for the service. Seven findings dismantle this, and the seventh is the most eloquent.

  1. Nowhere in the world is there a published tolling tariff for mine concentrate. The only published tariff in the entire sector is recycling: ReElement, in Indiana, charges US$ 25 to 35 per kilo to separate end-of-life magnets at 99.5% purity. For ore, what exists are purchases — with payability, a fixed price per contained REO, or a formula on Nd, Pr, Dy and Tb — or tolling embedded as a deduction inside an offtake, as in the Hastings–Neo deal.
  2. The historical test has already been run, and it failed. In 2013 Innovation Metals announced exactly this thesis: a central plant for toll separation of 7,500 t/yr in Bécancour, Quebec, with four letters of intent from miners. It never reached an investment decision. The company was absorbed by Ucore in 2020, which kept the technology and discarded the tolling model.
  3. "Any concentrate from any mine" is engineering fiction. CSIRO is explicit: a plant's parameters are "narrowly calibrated to a relatively homogeneous feedstock," and in ionic clays "each deposit has distinct chemical and mineralogical characteristics, requiring a customized desorption approach." The real mitigation is not universality — it is blending. And the empirical evidence is harsh: Lynas, with more than a decade of operation and single source, saw production fall because of ore variability and concentrate quality. If a single feed already destabilizes it, rotating feed from N mines is another problem entirely.
  4. Third parties' radiological liability stays in the refinery's country, forever. About one tonne of radioactive waste per tonne of rare earth produced. That is why Malaysia made the renewal of Lynas's license conditional on ending radioactive waste production within five years. A "bloc platform" is, in political terms, an invitation to import everyone else's liabilities.
  5. Without a benchmark, there is no way to price the service. There is no rare earths TC/RC, there is no terminal market, there is no fungible product — there are four disconnected price references (China EXW, China FOB, West CIF, Rotterdam). The tariff becomes pure bilateral bargaining power, against a counterparty that can take the material to China.
  6. Copper has already shown how the film ends. The copper concentrate treatment benchmark was negotiated at US$ 0 per tonne and 0 cents per pound for 2026 — the lowest in history — and spot reached about –US$ 90/t in March 2026: the miner pays the smelter to process. China went from ~15% to ~50% of global smelting; there remain two active smelters in the United States and a new plant costs about US$ 5 billion. The merchant refiner is the link that absorbs the overcapacity shock.
  7. The industry's revealed preference is unanimous. Energy Fuels bought Base Resources and ASM; Iluka buys Northern Minerals' concentrate; Carester signed an offtake with Brazilian Rare Earths; MP took equity in Ma'aden; Lindian bought the Kazakh plant instead of tolling through it. No one with real capital has chosen to be a pure service provider.
Where Idea 1 survives — and there are four concrete cases

In recycling, where the feed is more standardized, the lots are small and the customer wants its own metal back — it is the only niche with a published tariff. As an embedded fee inside an offtake, deducted from the payment to the miner. When the state pays for option value: the US Department of War finances MP's share of the Saudi JV on a non-recourse, and Export Finance Australia lent A$ 1.65 bn non-recourse to Iluka. And, above all, when the hub controls the anchor feedstock and sells only the marginal capacity — which is Iluka's real model at Eneabba, announced as an open hub and contracted as a buyer.

Translating this to Brazil: the platform refinery is not a commercial arbitrage business. It is sovereign infrastructure with captive feedstock, which occasionally sells spare capacity to third parties. That version is defensible. The "I take feed from anyone and charge a fee" version is not.

Idea 2 — Urban mining as a secondary monopoly partially correct, for the wrong reason

The thesis is right that tailings and scrap are the country's cheapest and fastest asset — and section 12 shows why, with the phosphogypsum at Uberaba. But the "monopoly on the hidden stockpile" argument needs two corrections.

The first is physics: rare earth recycling today is less than 1% and there is a lag of about twelve years between making the magnet and it becoming scrap. Even in an aggressive scenario, recycling covers ~8% of demand in 2030 — the European target of 25% is far out of reach. The real short-term feedstock is factory scrap, which corresponds to 20% to 30% of the material processed, not installed stock. Anyone conflating the two overestimates the market by an order of magnitude.

The second is good news: it is exactly in recycling that the platform model works. It is the only segment in the entire sector with a published service tariff. Idea 1 and Idea 2, therefore, fit better than the original version assumed — but inverted: the platform is born in recycling and tailings, not in mine concentrate.

Idea 3 — The data and certification layer the market exists, but it is not what it seems

This is the one that changed most with the research, and it earned a section of its own — the next one. The three-line summary: yes, the market has formed; none of the four players cited covers rare earths commercially and verifiably; and the premium that does exist is not "green", it is "non-China".

The paradox — and why it has already resolved itself in practice

The original objection is honest: building the clean refining fiefdom solves the national problem and reproduces the global logic being criticized, merely changing who collects the toll. The proposed way out — what if the fiefdom is not private? — is better than it looked when it was written, because is what is happening.

In 2026, virtually no separation capacity in the West was built as a purely private business. The U.S. Department of War holds 15% of MP Materials and guarantees the price through 2035; the U.S. government holds ~10% of USA Rare Earth; the Department of Commerce holds a stake in Vulcan; the Pentagon holds 40% of a JV with Korea Zinc; Export Finance Australia lent A$ 1.65 bn on a non-recourse basis to Iluka; Japan's JOGMEC put € 110 million into France's Caremag, which also received € 106 million from the French state. The mixed-control model is not an idealistic alternative to the market — it is the market.

What the sector analysis says, and it is worth quoting as is: the West shifted to preferred equity, debt, price floors and purchase commitments because it began treating separation as strategic infrastructure, not as a business. Whoever proposes the Brazilian refinery should propose it on those terms — not as a private capital return, which section 12 shows does not close without a premium.

In short
  • The pure platform refinery exists nowhere: there is no published tolling tariff for mine concentrate.
  • Where it works is with captive feedstock and public money — which is how all Western capacity was built.
  • Urban mining is real, but the near-term feedstock is factory scrap, not installed stock.
CHAPTER 10The market

The competitive map of certification

The market exists. The four names on the original map do not — at least not in rare earths.

The thesis that the certification layer has already left the drawing board is correct. What verification changed was who is in it and what exactly is sellable. Let us start with the correction, because it is a large one.

PlayerStatusWhat the verification found
ReSourcedoes not cover REE Covers cobalt, nickel, lithium and natural graphite. Rare earths do not appear anywhere of the company's material. And Glencore, CMOC and ERG are not customers — they are founders and core partners, alongside Umicore. The difference is material: the revenue is not sales to them, it is financing by them. No funding round, valuation or corporate structure has been disclosed.
Circularise + Minviro + REIA
(CSyARES)		became an LCA, not a seal Grundfos and BEC are not customers — they are partners in a consortium funded by EIT RawMaterials. The concrete deliverable was a PCR (product category rules) published by EPD International in 2024, valid through 2028: environmental footprint accounting rules, not an origin certification scheme with audit. It is voluntary and no regulator requires it. REIA changed CEO in September 2025 and is under strategic review.
NoviqTech (ASX:NVQ)irrelevant Revenue of AUD 3,317 in 2024 — a drop of 86% over the previous year. Sectors listed on the site: aviation, biofuels, hydrogen, batteries. No mention of critical minerals or rare earths. Micro-cap with no material revenue.
Everledgercollapsed Went into administration in Australia and liquidation in the United Kingdom in May 2023, after raising US$ 20 mn from Tencent. The founder took the company back with ~15 employees, focused on gems and textiles. And the association with MaDiTraCe not confirmed: the official partner list on CORDIS does not include it. The company in MaDiTraCe is Spherity — that one does, and covering neodymium.
Evolution Metalswrong category It is not a traceability company. It is a producer and integrator of "defense-compliant" magnets and metals that uses the DFARS deadline as a commercial narrative.
 Five names, five corrections. None of them is today a verified commercial supplier of rare earth traceability.

It is the admission that software alone does not sell compliance; it needs the signature of an accredited body.

The most underestimated finding: the standard already exists, and no one uses it

While the debate argues over who will write the rare earths traceability standard, ISO has already written it. The technical committee ISO/TC 298 published two standards that, together, close the entire chain:

  • ISO 23664:2021 — traceability of rare earths from the mine to the separated products.
  • ISO 17887:2025 — traceability from the separated products to the permanent magnets, published in August 2025. It specifies the documentation that makes it possible to identify which links processed a given shipment and validate sustainability, environmental impact and recycled content claims.

They are voluntary, they have no established certification body, and I did not find a single company claiming compliance with ISO 17887. For anyone seeking to anchor credibility cheaply, it is the cheapest institutional asset available today: being the first to certify against a standard that already exists is infinitely faster than creating a new label.

What actually binds, and when

Three corrections that change how the market reads:

  1. DFARS is a prohibition, not a traceability mandate. Clause 252.225-7052, backed by 10 U.S.C. § 4872, prohibits delivering samarium-cobalt or NdFeB magnets mined, refined, separated, melted or produced in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea from 01/01/2027. It does not ask for a certificate. The demand for proof comes from flow-down through several tiers of subcontracting and of False Claims Act risk. Whoever sells "DFARS compliance" is selling legal risk mitigation.

    And there is a real risk that the deadline changes: Section 1801 of the NDAA FY2027 proposes replacing the "mine-to-metal" restriction with a tiered domestic content regime. The House passed it on 22/07/2026 by 216 to 212; the cloture motion in the Senate failed on 14/07/2026. The law was not enacted. Any thesis anchored exclusively on 01/01/2027 carries regulatory risk in the coming months.

    The documentary obligation in fact came from somewhere else: the Executive Order of 20/07/2026, which mandates supply chain mapping and, according to secondary analysis, gives contractors 180 days to provide bills of materials tracing components back to the raw material source.
  2. The binding trigger on magnets is European, and it is the CRMA. Articles 28 and 29 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 require, for vehicles, wind turbines, heat pumps, MRI machines, industrial robots and household appliances with permanent magnets: indelible physical labeling, digital record accessible by QR or RFID with weight, location and chemical composition of the magnet, and disclosure of recycled content of neodymium, dysprosium, praseodymium and terbium for products with more than 0.2 kg of magnet. Application around first quarter of 2028, with a February 2026 proposal to extend it to household appliances and introduce recycled-content minimums from 2031.

    Note the nature of the obligation: it is product data, not proof of geographic origin. But proving recycled content requires custody — and it is through that crack that traceability enters.
  3. China already operates the most complete rare earth traceability system in the world. Since 01/10/2024, the Rare Earth Administration Regulation requires companies in mining, refining, separation, smelting and export to record product flow in a state system, with lot number, volume, sale date, specification and invoice, with monthly upload. It was built as export control instrument. The West is trying to build the same mechanism for the opposite purpose.
There is no "green rare earth" premium. There is a "non-China rare earth" premium

The LME covers aluminum, copper, nickel and zinc under the sustainable premium framework — does not list rare earths — and explicitly stated that cannot operationalize country-of-origin requirements, which is precisely the logic on which the entire critical minerals strategy rests. Argus has expanded its rare earth price coverage to the US and Europe, but these are material prices, not environmental premium assessments. There is no index, label or assessment for "green rare earth" with a publicly priced premium.

The premium that does exist is geopolitical: paying more for material that has not passed through China. That is the sellable product — and it is on that, not on carbon, that the Brazilian proposal should be built.

The oracle problem — and why it has not been solved yet

Every traceability architecture has the same blind spot: guaranteeing that the data was true at the input. The IEA says it in plain terms — "the lack of adequate verification mechanisms can lead to inaccurate or falsified data, undermining the very purpose of the system". IRMA goes further, and the criticism comes from within: traceability proves path, not proof practice; in the case it reports, an electronics brand traced the mineral to the specific mine and could verify nothing, because the mine refused to provide the documentation.

And for rare earths, chemistry does not solve it. The most advanced method published to date, out of MaDiTraCe in 2026, separates rare earths from iron-rich NdFeB magnets and shows remarkably stable distribution patterns along the chain — but the authors themselves note that "does not reliably determine geological origin on its own, because metallurgical processing alters elemental ratios", and that neodymium isotopic analysis will probably be required. The fingerprint analytical, from Germany's BGR, the sector reference, covers tin, tungsten and tantalum — does not cover rare earths — and the BGR itself warns that it should not be used as a standalone method for sourcing decisions.

The technical verdict, as of August 2026: there is no validated, scalable and commercially available method to prove the geographic origin of a rare earth inside a finished magnet. Chemistry is useful for checking batch consistency and detecting anomalous blending. It is not useful for answering "did this sample come from China?".

In Nzibira, South Kivu, the validated mines produced less than 20% of the roughly 83 tonnes of minerals that were tagged there in the first quarter of 2021. In Lubuhu, roughly fifteen times more more cassiterite was tagged than the two nearby validated mines produced in the quarter.

Global Witness, "The ITSCI Laundromat", 2022 — the largest scheme of due diligence of 3TG minerals from the Great Lakes region, removed from the list of mechanisms recognized by the Responsible Minerals Initiative in November of that year

This is the case any buyer or investor will cite back at a Brazilian certification proposal. A scheme with physical tagging, auditing and field presence tagged five to fifteen times more material than the validated mines produced. The tag does not validate origin; it validates that someone put a tag on it. Anyone who wants to build the certification layer has to answer that before anything else — and the answer cannot be software.

The defensible synthesis

The original conclusion — Idea 3 glued to Idea 1, because certification only has value if you own what makes it true — remains correct, and the research reinforces it by a different path than expected. It is not the clean electron that makes it true, because there is no carbon premium in rare earths. It is the physical control of the material: if the oxide is born inside your own plant, origin does not have to be proven by forensic chemistry — it is constitutive. Certifying someone else's chain is the hard business, with a precedent of fraud and no analytical method. Certifying your own material, against an ISO standard that already exists and nobody uses, is the easy business.

In one sentence: what is defensible is neither the data platform nor the service refinery — it is the refinery with captive feedstock that issues its own certificate, against ISO 17887, selling the "non-China" attribute that is already regulated, and not the "green" attribute that no one pays for.

CHAPTER 11The proof

The proof layer

Who is trying to solve the oracle, with how much money, and what survives verification.

The previous section ended in a deadlock: traceability proves path, not practice, and for rare earths there is no validated method of proving geographic origin. This section maps who is attacking that problem — including the Brazilian bet — and holds every claim in the positioning material to the same yardstick applied to the rest of the document. Seven claims did not hold up, and they are corrected throughout the text.

11.1 The five layers, and where the hole is

The competition is not a list of trackers. They are layers attacking the same problem by different routes, and each one is blind exactly where the other sees.

  • Oracles and DePIN — they bring real-world data onto the chain. Chainlink, with about US$ 6 billion in market cap, verifies that reserves reported match the tokens issued; it pulls data from custodians and auditors, but does not independently audit the physical existence of the asset. DePIN networks prove physical work (coverage, storage), not the truth of origin. Scale caveat: the US$ 9 to 20 billion cited for DePIN are token market cap — the sector's real on-chain revenue is on the order of US$ 72 million a year, a 260-fold difference.
  • Physical proof by laboratory — they test the atom itself. It is the only layer that solves "garbage in" through science and not through a seal, and it is the head-on threat.
  • Traceability and passport — chain of custody and mass balance. They fully inherit the oracle problem, as section 10 showed.
  • Standard, carbon and token anchoring — they write the ruler, measure the green or move the token. All of them need proof underneath.
  • Adjacent markets with the same pain — carbon and gold. And here is the data point that most validates the thesis: the investigation by Guardian, of the Die Zeit and SourceMaterial, from January 2023, concluded that about 94% of the REDD+ credits analyzed in Verra-certified projects did not represent real emission reductions. Verra challenged the synthetic controls methodology. It is the same origin problem, in a billion-dollar market.

11.2 What verification corrected

Seven claims in the positioning material do not survive the fact-check. They matter because they are exactly the ones a skeptical investor or buyer will test first.

Oritain covers rare earthswrong Oritain covers agricultural and natural commodities — cotton, leather, timber, meat, coffee, wool, cocoa, palm, soy. Not even its science page mentions metals or minerals. It is entry potential, not installed competition — which changes the reading from "frontal threat" to "open door".

11.3 The size of the enemy

It is the question the material raised and it is worth answering with a number, because it defines who you compete against for capital and for customers.

11.4 The four axes, tested

The material's central thesis is that each rival dominates at most one axis, and that the intersection of the four is open territory. The thesis is confirmed on the negative side — no one combines all four. But the affirmative part needs a correction of degree: Lastre has one full axis and three partial, not four full ones.

Each one is worth detailing, because the difference between "we have" and "we are positioned to have" is what separates a thesis from a pitch.

  1. True at the input — partial, and it is the existential risk. The label proves that that reading did not change afterward. It does not prove that the operator did not point the sensor at the clean ore and ship the dirty one. The material itself acknowledges this and proposes the right answer: seal the isotopic report from Oritain or SourceCertain instead of competing with them. That is the play, and it is even better than it looked — because Oritain does not cover rare earths, so there is no overlap. The move is complementary, not competitive.
  2. Quantum-safe — partial, and the label needs to change. The Casper × AmericanFortress partnership of 04/08/2026 is real. But the scheme is not "ZKPoSP — zero-knowledge post-quantum protection": it is Post-Quantum Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets, published on IACR ePrint on 21/07/2026. And the stage is roadmap: Casper's CTO states an intention to adopt, with milestones "to be announced", and the network's own roadmap puts quantum-safe signatures in 2027. The honest formulation is the one the material itself already uses in a footnote — positioned to be natively quantum-safe, not "already is today".

    And the yardstick is narrower than assumed: CNSA 2.0 does not "require post-quantum cryptography from 2027" — what exists on 01/01/2027 is a acquisition gate for US national security systems. The European 2030 target applies to critical infrastructure. These are real requirements, but sectoral.
  3. Green label + non-China — partial, and the adjective is inverted. Section 10 showed that there is no "green rare earth" premium: the LME covers four base metals and refuses to operationalize a country criterion; there is no index or label with a priced premium. What does exist, and is regulated, is the premium for non-China origin. The sellable product is "non-China" with "green" as an accessory compliance attribute — not the other way around. That inversion strengthens the thesis rather than weakening it, because "non-China" has a buyer compelled by a defense contract; "green" does not.
  4. Agent-native — covered, and it is the most solid axis of the set. x402 is a Linux Foundation standard, created by Coinbase, with the foundation's operational launch in July 2026 and 40 member organizations, among them Google, Stripe and Visa. And the facilitator is live on Casper mainnet since 04/06/2026. Unlike almost everything else on the Casper side — ProofLayer with no announcement date, ERC-3643 "once fully implemented", ZKPoSP on the roadmap — this one is in production.

11.5 Who controls whether the label matters

The right question, and the answer is not the competitors: it is the standards and the State. Here the material is dead right, and there is one finding that deserves highlighting because it is the only complete precedent that exists.

The gold precedent — verified and solid

A LBMA named aXedras, of Zug, as the official provider of the Gold Bar Integrity Database in March 2024. By the end of 2025, all refiners on the Good Delivery List were integrated. Voluntary country-of-origin reporting began in April 2026 and the mandatory monthly reporting takes effect in 2027.

In other words: in a market with the same origin problem, a private standards association chose a technical provider, integrated 100% of the participants and is making reporting mandatory — all in three years. It is the proof that the play "feed the standard before trying to be the standard" works. And it is also the warning: that slot has already been filled in gold. The equivalent window in critical minerals is still open because the standard has not been written — ISO 17887 has existed since August 2025 and has no established certification body, and the G7 put rare earths in the queue for traceability pilots, behind lithium and nickel.

The other owners of the yardstick, with each one's real status: the EU Digital Product Passport Registry went live in 20/07/2026, governed by Implementing Regulation 2026/1778, with a mandated API — but it is an empty shell for now, because no product category has a mandatory passport yet and the battery one only applies from February 2027. The ANM, in Brazil, has already said it wants origin traceability to counter CFEM evasion, and it is the most obvious and least contested anchor customer. And IRMA defines good practice by audit, not by technology — entry there is through accreditation, not through product.

This is the item that determines whether the thesis is defensible.
What stops Circulor from copying it in six months? Circulor has Volvo, Trafigura, Bureau Veritas and TÜV, and already plugs into the certifiers. The reading of about eighteen months is plausible — with the caveat that the DFARS deadline may change before then, and that the gold slot has already been taken.
What is left after the fact-check

The negative thesis is confirmed in full: no one combines all four axes, none of the traceability players covers rare earths on a commercial, verified basis, and the oracle has not been solved for rare earths by any method. The territory exists.

The affirmative thesis needs two corrections of degree, and both make it more defensible, not less. First: the product is "non-China" with green as an accessory, not "green" — because it is the first one with a buyer compelled by regulation. Second: the anchor cannot be cryptographic, it has to be physical — and the route is already mapped, because Oritain, the best in the world at this, does not cover rare earths and therefore is not a rival. The model to copy is Tracr: physical proof, plus on-chain registry, plus a reference institution as a partner. It was exactly this arrangement that the GIA bought 30% of in May 2026.

In short
  • None of the four players on the original map covers rare earths commercially and verifiably.
  • The traceability standard already exists — ISO 23664 and ISO 17887 — and no company claims conformity.
  • The oracle is not solved: metallurgical processing erases the material's origin signature.
CHAPTER 12The math

The economics of the thesis

What it costs, what it yields, and under what condition it closes.

The entire Brazilian discussion of rare earths takes place without a calculation. This section does the calculation — explicitly simplified and with stated assumptions, so that it can be contested rather than merely rhetorical.

The reference module estimate

A complete national module processing 5,000 t/yr of TREO in mixed concentrate — roughly Serra Verde's Phase 1 capacity — from concentrate to sintered magnet. Typical composition of Brazilian ionic clay: NdPr ~1,125 t, Dy ~50 t, Tb ~10 t, yttrium ~600 t, lanthanum, cerium and others ~3,215 t, all on an oxide basis.

Two conversions, stated so that the math can be redone: oxide → metal at 0.85 kg per kg (oxygen is about 15% of the mass of the oxide) and NdFeB magnet with 30% metallic NdPr by mass. Hence 1,125 t of NdPr oxide yield 956 t of metal and 3,190 t of magnet per year. Dysprosium and terbium are consumed inside the magnet; yttrium, lanthanum and cerium are sold separately.

StepCapacityCAPEX (range)CentralComparables used
Oxide separation5,000 t/a TREOUS$ 550–750 mnUS$ 650 mn Aclara Dynamo US$ 212 thousand/t·a · Rainbow Phalaborwa US$ 158 thousand/t·a · Energy Fuels Phase 2 ~US$ 65 thousand/t·a · Iluka Eneabba ~US$ 65 thousand/t·a
NdFeB metal and alloy~3,190 t/yUS$ 150–210 mnUS$ 177 mn Aclara: US$ 149 mn for 2,681 t/a of NdFeB alloy → US$ 56 thousand/t·a, same basis (alloy, not metal)

Separation of heavies is an order of magnitude more expensive: Energy Fuels' commercial plant in Utah costs ~US$ 104 mn for 120 t/a of Dy and 20 t/a of Tb — US$ 743 thousand per annual tonne.

The revenue, and what moving up the value chain actually adds

Sales form for the same outputAnnual gross revenue
Mixed concentrate (MREC), at 50% payability on contained oxide~US$ 79 mn
Separated oxides~US$ 157 mn
Sintered magnets (3,190 t at US$ 85/kg) + yttrium, lanthanum and cerium~US$ 281 mn
 Prices used for the oxides: NdPr US$ 110/kg, Dy US$ 250/kg, Tb US$ 1,100/kg, yttrium US$ 9/kg, lanthanum, cerium and others US$ 1.5/kg — the last two add up to US$ 10.2 mn and are the only revenue that survives outside the magnet. Incremental OPEX: US$ 125 mn/year in separation (US$ 25/kg of TREO) and US$ 64 mn/year in metal and magnet (~US$ 20/kg of magnet). The magnet realization price of US$ 85/kg is an own derivation — there is no reliable public price series for NdFeB magnets — and it is the dominant variable of the whole model. estimate

Netting out OPEX and the opportunity value of the concentrate, the incremental EBITDA gain from moving up the value chain is US$ 3.2 million a year for every dollar per kilo in the magnet realization price, less US$ 257 million of fixed cost of the structure. The deciding variable is not the NdPr price — it is at what price the Brazilian magnet is sold:

The break-even points

Solving for the magnet realization price that equates incremental EBITDA to the annual return required by the US$ 1.07 billion CAPEX:

RequirementRequired annual returnBreakeven magnetRequired premium
Generating cash only, without remunerating capitalUS$ 0US$ 81/kgnone
Concessional capital + 20% tax credit (PL 2780)US$ 67 mnUS$ 102/kg~20%
BNDES/FINEP concessional capital (6% p.a., 25 years)US$ 83 mnUS$ 107/kg~26%
Market cost of capital (12% p.a. real, 20 years)US$ 143 mnUS$ 126/kg~48%
Realization reference used in the modelUS$ 85/kg—
Premium paid outside China on separated oxides—25% to 67%
 Dominant sensitivity: the magnet realization price, at US$ 3.2 mn/year per dollar/kg — the difference between market capital and concessional capital is worth US$ 19/kg of magnet. The NdPr price matters less than it appears, because it enters both sides of the calculation: it raises the cost of the input and the value of the product at the same time. The entire table is our own derivation; changes in ore composition, payability, OPEX or either of the two conversions shift every point.
What the numbers say, in one sentence

The domestic chain generates cash above US$ 81 per kilo of magnet, remunerates concessional capital above US$ 107 and market capital above US$ 126. With the tax credit, the requirement falls to US$ 102. In other words: the distance between unviable and viable is a realization premium of 20% to 48% — within the 25% to 67% range that the market outside China already practices on separated oxides, and of the same family as the US$ 110/kg NdPr floor that the US, Japan and Australia built.

Two conclusions follow. First: the constraint is not capital — the annual gap is US$ 70 to 130 million per module, not billions, and it falls to zero if the premium is captured. Second: the instrument that closes the gap is price, not capital injection — floor, long-term offtake or public procurement. It is what Brazil does not have, it is what Serra Verde handed to a US SPV for fifteen years, and it is the obvious quid pro quo to demand from whoever wants access to the Brazilian asset.

National scale. If every announced Brazilian project reaches capacity, the country would process on the order of 30,000 t/yr of TREO around 2035 — six reference modules. The same arithmetic implies about US$ 470 mn/yr of revenue selling concentrate, ~US$ 945 mn/yr selling separated oxides and ~US$ 1.7 bn/yr selling magnets, with aggregate CAPEX of US$ 5 to 8 billion (central ~US$ 6.4 bn) over a decade. For comparison, BNDES and FINEP have already pre-selected R$ 45.8 billion — about US$ 8.5 billion. The money exists on paper. What does not exist is the price condition that makes it investable.

In short
  • Verticalizing a 5,000 t/yr module costs US$ 1.07 bn and only remunerates market capital with the magnet at US$ 126/kg.
  • The deciding variable is not the NdPr price — it is the magnet realization price, at US$ 3.2 mn per dollar/kg.
  • The instrument that closes the gap is price, not capital: a floor, an offtake or public procurement.

The graveyard of Western projects is large, and the lessons are replicable in Brazil.

It is the only defense that works, and it is precisely the one Brazil does not have. That is why every dollar of real money that has entered the sector in Brazil — DFC, EXIM, Vision Blue, EMG, Denham — is foreign, which produces exactly the Serra Verde outcome. Separation is a standalone chemical project: add 2 to 4 years and US$ 300–400 mn for a 2,000 t/a plant, US$ 550–750 mn for a 5,000 t/a one. Prioritize routes that skip the mine: phosphogypsum, tailings, recycling of factory scrap.
Permitting and litigation Law 15.190/2025 came into force on 04/02/2026 and is already under an ADI at the STF — ADIs 7.913, 7.916 and 7.919, filed by APIB, PSOL, PV, Rede and ANAMMA, with Alexandre de Moraes as rapporteur — precisely on the points that matter to mining, the LAC and the LAE. And the ruling was scheduled for August 12, 2026, four days after this document's cut-off date. Anyone using the special license before then is betting on a result that lands this week. The new law did not reduce risk: it moved it from the environmental agency to the STF. Treating social and environmental compliance as a financing condition at the first phase, not the second.
Prior consultation Bolivia has the world's largest lithium reserves, signed US$ 2 bn with China and Russia — and lost everything to a citizen suit by 53 indigenous communities for lack of adequate prior consultation; contracts suspended since May 2025 and still halted. PL 2780 speaks of "continuous dialogue", not of free, prior and informed consultation. Consultation under Convention 169 is capital risk reducer, not cost. Note: 187 rare earth mining claims overlap with 96 land-reform settlements in five states.
State-owned, without the technology LitioMx: four years, ~MXN 50 mn spent (90% on payroll), zero funds budgeted for exploration, zero grams produced and ICSID arbitration filed by Ganfeng. Declaring a resource strategic and creating a state company creates neither technical capability, nor technology, nor capital. The test question for any "Terrabras": who pays the US$ 550–750 mn for separation, who masters solvent extraction, and what happens if the next election changes the rule. Ironic note: Brazil already has a state-owned company in the nuclear link — INB — and it is INB that holds the monazite monopoly.
Losing the value link Chile, copper: from 14.6% of world smelting in 1990 (world leader) to ~6% in 2024, while China went to ~45%. Today it exports 2.6 Mt of unprocessed concentrate, and refined output is projected to fall from 52% to 21% of copper exports by 2035. Gold, silver, molybdenum, rhenium, selenium and tellurium go with it — every by-product stays in the country that smelts. Chile is Brazil in rare earths, thirty years ahead. With one difference: Chilean copper has scale, liquidity and an LME price. Rare earths have an opaque market and a price set in China. Chile lost margin; Brazil could lose the entire product.
Criminal capture In Colombia, ~85% of gold is illegal and generates US$ 8.4 bn/year — more than drug trafficking. Armed groups went from 13 thousand to 27 thousand members and are already migrating from gold to critical minerals. High-value, low-volume rare earths are transportable. Origin traceability from the outset, before the problem exists.
